metadata.title: B2: Grassroots Engagement
metadata.description: The democratic-renewal loop. Falling trust mobilizes citizen organizing. Small-dollar platforms (ActBlue, WinRed) make candidates viable without big donors. Competition forces responsiveness. The post-2008 small-donor revolution is the contemporary example.
metadata.author: US Government Intelligent Textbook

nodes.label: Trust In Government
nodes.description: The percentage of citizens who say they trust the federal government to do what is right.

nodes.label: Grassroots Activism
nodes.description: Citizen-led organizing — door-knocking, voter registration drives, advocacy networks — that builds political power from below.

nodes.label: Small-Donor Participation
nodes.description: Campaign fundraising from contributions under $200. ActBlue and WinRed have made this competitive at scale.

nodes.label: Competitive Elections
nodes.description: Races where the outcome is not predetermined — multiple viable candidates, real debate, voters whose choices matter.

nodes.label: Perceived Responsiveness
nodes.description: Citizens' sense that elected officials actually hear and act on their concerns.

edges.description: Falling trust mobilizes citizen organizing — people show up when they feel the system has failed.
Activists give small donations and recruit others to do the same.
Small-dollar funded candidates can compete without depending on major donors.
Competition forces incumbents to actually listen to constituents.
When citizens see officials responding to their concerns, trust rises.

loops.label: B2: Grassroots Engagement
loops.description: The most hopeful loop in the diagram — the democratic-renewal counter to R1–R4.
